```{r setup, message=FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
library(p8105.datasets)
library(patchwork)
```

# Problem 1: NY NOAA

## Data description

```{r load-noaa}
library(p8105.datasets)
data("ny_noaa")

ny_noaa
```



The ny_noaa dataset contains daily weather observations from weather stations across New York State. It includes station identifiers, observation dates, precipitation, snowfall, snow depth, maximum temperature, and minimum temperature. The dataset contains 2,595,176 observations and 7 variables. Missing data may be an issue because some weather measurements are not recorded for every station on every day.


```{r clean-noaa}
# Separate the date into year, month, and day
noaa_clean =
  ny_noaa |>
  separate(date, into = c("year", "month", "day"), sep = "-") |>
  mutate(
    # Convert date components to integers
    year = as.integer(year),
    month = as.integer(month),
    day = as.integer(day),

    # Convert precipitation from tenths of mm to mm
    prcp = prcp / 10,

    # Convert temperatures from tenths of degrees Celsius
    tmax = as.numeric(tmax) / 10,
    tmin = as.numeric(tmin) / 10,

    # Keep snowfall and snow depth in their original units
    snow = as.numeric(snow),
    snwd = as.numeric(snwd)
  )

# Check the cleaned dataset
noaa_clean
```
```{r snowfall-frequency}
# Count the frequency of each snowfall value
noaa_clean |>
  count(snow, sort = TRUE) |>
  slice_head(n = 10)
```
The most common recorded snowfall value is 0, with 2,008,508 observations. This is reasonable because snowfall does not occur on most station-days. There are also 381,221 missing observations, indicating that snowfall was not recorded for every station-day. Other common values, such as 25 mm and 13 mm, represent recorded snowfall amounts.


```{r}
# Calculate the proportion of missing values in each variable
missing_summary <- noaa_clean |>
  summarize(across(everything(), ~ mean(is.na(.x))))

# Display the results
missing_summary
```
The proportion of missing values varies across variables. Precipitation has approximately 5.62% missing values, while snowfall and snow depth have approximately 14.69% and 22.80% missing values, respectively. Maximum and minimum temperatures have approximately 43.71% missing values each. The station identifier and date components have no missing values. This indicates that missingness is particularly substantial for temperature measurements and should be considered when interpreting the results.


## Average maximum temperature in January and July


```{r jan-july-temp}
# Calculate average maximum temperature by station, year, and month
noaa_monthly = noaa_clean |>
  filter(month %in% c(1, 7)) |>
  group_by(id, year, month) |>
  summarize(
    mean_tmax = mean(tmax, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  filter(!is.nan(mean_tmax))

# Plot January and July temperatures across years
ggplot(noaa_monthly, aes(x = year, y = mean_tmax, group = id)) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.08) +
  facet_wrap(~month, ncol = 2,
             labeller = labeller(month = c("1" = "January",
                                           "7" = "July"))) +
  labs(
    title = "Average Maximum Temperature by Station",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Mean Maximum Temperature (°C)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```
Interpretation: The average maximum temperature is substantially higher in July than in January across weather stations. January temperatures are generally near or below 0°C, whereas July temperatures are mostly around 25–30°C. This reflects the seasonal differences in New York State. There is variation across stations and years, with some unusually low or high values that may represent outliers or unusual weather conditions.

## Temperature relationship and snowfall distributions



```{r temp-snow-plots}
# Plot 1: Relationship between maximum and minimum temperature
temp_plot <- noaa_clean |>
  filter(!is.na(tmax), !is.na(tmin)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = tmin, y = tmax)) +
  geom_bin2d() +
  labs(
    title = "Maximum vs Minimum Temperature",
    x = "Minimum Temperature (°C)",
    y = "Maximum Temperature (°C)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()


# Plot 2: Snowfall distribution by year
snow_plot <- noaa_clean |>
  filter(!is.na(snow), snow > 0, snow < 100) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = factor(year), y = snow)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.alpha = 0.2) +
  labs(
    title = "Snowfall Distribution by Year",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Snowfall (mm)"
  ) +
  scale_x_discrete(breaks = seq(1980, 2010, by = 5)) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1, size = 8))


# Display both plots side by side

temp_plot + snow_plot
```


Interpretation: Maximum and minimum temperatures show a positive association, meaning that days with higher minimum temperatures generally also have higher maximum temperatures. The binned plot reveals a dense central cluster and a few observations that may be outliers.

Snowfall distributions vary across years. The plot shows the distribution of positive snowfall measurements below 100 mm for each year. Zero snowfall and values of 100 mm or greater are excluded to focus on smaller snowfall amounts. The boxplots allow comparison of yearly distributions, but the large number of years makes individual differences difficult to distinguish.

# Problem 2: NHANES

## Import and clean the data

```{r load-nhanes}
# Import demographics data, skipping the four introductory rows
nhanes_covar <- read_csv(
  "data/nhanes_covar.csv",
  skip = 5,
  col_names = c("seqn", "sex", "age", "bmi", "education"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
) |>
  mutate(
    seqn = as.numeric(seqn),
    sex = as.numeric(sex),
    age = as.numeric(age),
    bmi = as.numeric(bmi),
    education = as.numeric(education)
  )

# Import accelerometer data
nhanes_accel <- read_csv(
  "data/nhanes_accel.csv",
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

# Check the data
glimpse(nhanes_covar)
head(nhanes_covar)
head(nhanes_accel[, 1:6])
```

```{r clean-merge-nhanes}
# Convert sex and education to labeled factors
nhanes_covar <- nhanes_covar |>
  mutate(
    sex = factor(
      sex,
      levels = c(1, 2),
      labels = c("Male", "Female")
    ),
    education = factor(
      education,
      levels = c(1, 2, 3),
      labels = c(
        "Less than high school",
        "High school equivalent",
        "More than high school"
      ),
      ordered = TRUE
    )
  )

# Merge demographics with minute-by-minute activity data
nhanes_merged <- nhanes_covar |>
  inner_join(nhanes_accel, by = c("seqn" = "SEQN"))

# Check the merged dataset
glimpse(nhanes_merged)
dim(nhanes_merged)
```

```{r filter-nhanes}
# Keep participants age 21 or older with complete demographic data
nhanes_clean <- nhanes_merged |>
  filter(
    age >= 21,
    !is.na(sex),
    !is.na(age),
    !is.na(bmi),
    !is.na(education)
  )

# Check the filtered dataset
dim(nhanes_clean)

# Summarize the demographic variables
nhanes_clean |>
  summarize(
    participants = n(),
    minimum_age = min(age),
    maximum_age = max(age),
    missing_sex = sum(is.na(sex)),
    missing_age = sum(is.na(age)),
    missing_bmi = sum(is.na(bmi)),
    missing_education = sum(is.na(education))
  )
```

## Gender and education distribution

```{r education-table}
# Count participants by sex and education level
nhanes_clean |>
  count(education, sex) |>
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = sex,
    values_from = n,
    values_fill = 0
  )
```

The distribution of participants varies across education levels. In the less-than-high-school group, the numbers of males and females are similar (27 males and 28 females). In the high-school-equivalent group, there are more males than females (35 versus 23). In the more-than-high-school group, the numbers are also similar (56 males and 59 females). Overall, the largest group of participants has more than a high school education.

## Age distributions by sex and education

```{r age-distributions}
ggplot(nhanes_clean, aes(x = age, fill = sex)) +
  geom_histogram(
    binwidth = 5,
    position = "identity",
    alpha = 0.5
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~education, ncol = 1) +
  labs(
    title = "Age Distribution by Sex and Education Level",
    x = "Age (years)",
    y = "Number of Participants",
    fill = "Sex"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```
The age distributions show how participants are distributed across age groups, separately by sex and education level. Participants span ages 21 to 80 years. The number and age distribution of males and females vary across education groups, although the histograms overlap. Because the sample sizes differ across education groups, differences in bar heights should be interpreted in the context of the number of participants in each group.

## Total physical activity by age and sex

```{r total-activity}
# Calculate total activity across all 1440 minutes
nhanes_clean <- nhanes_clean |>
  mutate(
    total_activity = rowSums(
      across(starts_with("min")),
      na.rm = TRUE
    )
  )

# Plot total activity against age, by sex and education
ggplot(
  nhanes_clean,
  aes(x = age, y = total_activity, color = sex)
) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", se = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(~education, ncol = 1) +
  labs(
    title = "Total Physical Activity by Age, Sex, and Education",
    x = "Age (years)",
    y = "Total Activity (sum of minute-level MIMS)",
    color = "Sex"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

Total physical activity varies across participants of different ages, sexes, and education levels. The scatterplots show substantial variation in activity among people of the same age. The smoothed curves suggest that activity generally decreases at older ages in several groups, although the pattern is not identical across education levels or between males and females. These patterns are descriptive and do not establish that age, sex, or education causes differences in physical activity.

## Activity patterns over 24 hours

```{r daily-activity}
# Calculate average activity at each minute of the day
activity_by_minute <- nhanes_clean |>
  select(sex, education, starts_with("min")) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = starts_with("min"),
    names_to = "minute",
    values_to = "activity"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    minute = as.integer(str_remove(minute, "min"))
  ) |>
  group_by(sex, education, minute) |>
  summarize(
    mean_activity = mean(activity, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# Plot average activity throughout the day
ggplot(
  activity_by_minute,
  aes(x = minute, y = mean_activity, color = sex)
) +
  geom_line() +
  facet_wrap(~education, ncol = 1) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = c(1, 240, 480, 720, 960, 1200, 1440),
    labels = c("12 AM", "4 AM", "8 AM", "12 PM",
               "4 PM", "8 PM", "12 AM")
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Average Activity Patterns Across 24 Hours",
    x = "Time of Day",
    y = "Mean Minute-Level MIMS",
    color = "Sex"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

The 24-hour activity profiles show a similar general pattern across education groups. Mean activity is relatively low overnight, increases sharply during the morning, remains elevated through much of the daytime, and decreases toward midnight. The curves for males and females are generally similar, although some differences are visible at particular times of day and across education groups. These results describe average activity patterns in this sample rather than proving that the groups differ in the broader population.

## Problem 3: CitiBike

### Import and clean the data

```{r}
citibike_jan2020 <- read_csv("data/citibike/Jan 2020 Citi.csv.zip", show_col_types = FALSE)
citibike_jan2024 <- read_csv("data/citibike/Jan 2024 Citi.csv.zip", show_col_types = FALSE)
citibike_july2020 <- read_csv("data/citibike/July 2020 Citi.csv.zip", show_col_types = FALSE)
citibike_july2024 <- read_csv("data/citibike/July 2024 Citi.csv.zip", show_col_types = FALSE)

glimpse(citibike_jan2020)
glimpse(citibike_jan2024)
glimpse(citibike_july2020)
glimpse(citibike_july2024)
```

### Combine and clean the data

```{r}
citibike_all <- bind_rows(
  citibike_jan2020 |> mutate(month = "January", year = 2020),
  citibike_jan2024 |> mutate(month = "January", year = 2024),
  citibike_july2020 |> mutate(month = "July", year = 2020),
  citibike_july2024 |> mutate(month = "July", year = 2024)
)

glimpse(citibike_all)
dim(citibike_all)
names(citibike_all)
```

### Inspect and clean the data

```{r}
summary(citibike_all$duration)

citibike_all |>
  count(month, year)

citibike_all |>
  count(member_casual)

citibike_all |>
  count(rideable_type)

citibike_all |>
  count(weekdays)
```

### Filter rides and take a 1% sample

```{r}
# Inspect duration units and values
summary(citibike_all$duration)

# Check whether duration is measured in minutes or hours
head(citibike_all$duration, 10)

# Keep rides under 4 hours and take a reproducible 1% sample
set.seed(123)

citibike_sample <- citibike_all |>
  filter(duration < 240)

# Check the resulting sample
dim(citibike_sample)
summary(citibike_sample$duration)
```

### Describe the sample

```{r}
citibike_sample |>
  summarize(
    total_rides = n(),
    median_duration = median(duration, na.rm = TRUE),
    mean_duration = mean(duration, na.rm = TRUE),
    min_duration = min(duration, na.rm = TRUE),
    max_duration = max(duration, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

citibike_sample |>
  count(year, month, member_casual)
```

### Ride counts by year, month, and membership

```{r}
ride_counts <- citibike_sample |>
  count(year, month, member_casual) |>
  arrange(year, factor(month, levels = c("January", "July")), member_casual)

ride_counts
```

### Top five start stations in July 2024


```{r}
top_stations_july2024 <- citibike_july2024 |>
  count(start_station_name, sort = TRUE) |>
  slice_head(n = 5)

top_stations_july2024
```

### Ride duration by day of the week

```{r}
citibike_sample |>
  mutate(
    weekdays = factor(
      weekdays,
      levels = c("Monday", "Tuesday", "Wednesday", "Thursday",
                 "Friday", "Saturday", "Sunday")
    )
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = weekdays, y = duration)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(
    title = "CitiBike Ride Duration by Day of the Week",
    x = "Day of the Week",
    y = "Ride Duration (minutes)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```


The boxplot compares CitiBike ride durations across the days of the week. The distributions show the typical ride duration, variability, and potential outliers for each day. Differences in the medians would suggest that typical ride duration varies by day, while differences in the interquartile ranges indicate variation in ride duration. The outliers represent rides that are substantially longer than most rides. These results describe associations and do not establish why ride durations differ across days.

### Ride duration by month and year

```{r}
citibike_sample |>
  mutate(
    month = factor(month, levels = c("January", "July"))
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = month, y = duration)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  facet_wrap(~year) +
  labs(
    title = "CitiBike Ride Duration by Month and Year",
    x = "Month",
    y = "Ride Duration (minutes)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```
The boxplots compare ride durations in January and July, separately for 2020 and 2024. Comparing the medians and spreads helps identify whether typical ride duration and variability differ between the two months within each year. Differences between 2020 and 2024 may also be visible. These comparisons are descriptive and do not establish the reasons for any observed differences.

### Ride duration by year

```{r}
citibike_sample |>
  ggplot(aes(x = factor(year), y = duration)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(
    title = "CitiBike Ride Duration by Year",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Ride Duration (minutes)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```
The boxplot compares ride-duration distributions between 2020 and 2024. Differences in the medians indicate differences in typical ride duration, while the box heights and whiskers show differences in variability. Potential outliers represent unusually long rides relative to the rest of the observations. Because the data include only January and July, the comparison does not necessarily represent ride durations across every month of either year.

### 2024 ride duration by month, membership, and bike type

```{r}
citibike_sample |>
  filter(year == 2024) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = month, y = duration, fill = member_casual)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  facet_wrap(~rideable_type) +
  labs(
    title = "2024 CitiBike Ride Duration by Month, Membership, and Bike Type",
    x = "Month",
    y = "Ride Duration (minutes)",
    fill = "Membership Type"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

This plot compares ride durations in January and July 2024 by membership type, with separate panels for bike type. Comparing the boxplots allows us to examine whether typical ride duration and variability differ by month, between casual and member riders, and across bike types. Any differences should be interpreted descriptively, since the plot alone cannot establish what caused them.
